title: Put routing and quota in the APIM policy layer, not in a service
context: Two product lines needed per-tenant rate limiting, routing, caching, schema validation and token injection in front of a shared GraphQL endpoint. The client mandate was explicit: no custom middleware unless required. Earlier testing had already produced an App Service single-instance failure.
decision: Implement the whole edge layer as Azure APIM policy XML — product routing for /ucc360 and /iline, rate-limit-by-key per tenant, response caching, schema validation and Bearer-token injection.

alternatives.option: Azure Functions in front of the endpoint
alternatives.why: Rejected — a custom middleware tier is exactly what the mandate excluded, and it adds a deploy pipeline and a cold-start profile to the request path.
Rejected — most operational surface of the three, and nothing in the requirement justified running containers to apply a rate limit.
Rejected on evidence — single-instance failure observed during earlier testing.

consequence: Policy XML has no real local debugger and is harder to unit test than application code. Accepted, because it removed an entire tier that could fail at 3am for a platform billing external customers.

title: Managed Identity over Service Principal
context: Service-to-service auth across the Fabric Lakehouse, APIM and downstream Azure resources, with a partner gateway in the path and multiple engineering teams touching the deployment.
decision: Managed Identity as the default identity model, with the rejected options written down alongside so the choice stays reviewable.

alternatives.why: Rejected — a secret that must be rotated is a secret that will eventually not be rotated, and it has to live somewhere.
Rejected — better than a secret, but still shifts lifecycle management onto a team that has no reason to own it.

consequence: Ties the platform more tightly to Azure-native identity, which is a real portability cost. Acceptable for a Fabric-based platform that is not leaving Azure.

title: One GraphQL endpoint for both product lines
context: Two product lines, ucc_360 and iline, selling access to the same Lakehouse Gold layer to external customers, through a partner gateway, with a consumer expectation that it 'feels like REST'.
decision: Expose a single GraphQL endpoint over the Gold layer and differentiate the products at the gateway policy layer rather than in the service.

alternatives.option: A REST service per product line
alternatives.why: Rejected — two codebases drifting apart around one schema, and the second product would have paid the integration cost again from scratch.

alternatives.option: One REST service with product query params
alternatives.why: Rejected — pushes shape negotiation onto every consumer and gets you a bespoke response contract per customer within a year.

consequence: Consumers who wanted REST got a gateway that behaves like it, while the platform kept one schema to evolve. The GraphQL surface needs disciplined depth and complexity limits, enforced at the policy layer.

title: Deduplicate scanner findings on embeddings, not rules
context: SAST, DAST and Git Leak each report the same underlying vulnerability in different vocabulary, with different severity opinions. Raw union of three reports is unreadable and goes untriaged.
decision: Embed every finding into Qdrant and deduplicate on vector similarity, then group across tools and assign one AI-scored severity from five classes.

alternatives.why: Rejected — only two of the three scanners emit reliable identifiers, and the overlap that matters most is described in prose.

alternatives.option: Exact string matching on file and line
alternatives.why: Rejected — DAST reports endpoints, SAST reports source locations. They rarely agree on a coordinate for the same issue.

consequence: Similarity thresholds are a judgement call with no correct answer. Tuned deliberately toward keeping duplicates rather than merging them, because a report that hides a CRITICAL is worthless in a way a repetitive one is not.

title: Recursive Language Model instead of flat retrieval
context: Document QA over long documents where every answer must come from the supplied scope. Flat top-k retrieval was returning locally relevant chunks that did not carry enough surrounding context to answer correctly.
decision: Introduce a Recursive Language Model to decompose long documents progressively rather than retrieving a flat window.

alternatives.why: Rejected — more chunks, more noise, and the answer got harder to ground rather than easier.
Rejected — trades precision for coverage and pushes cost up on every single query, including the easy ones.

consequence: More model calls per hard question. Paid for by keeping the scope guarantee intact, which is the entire reason the system is deployable in a compliance setting.

title: Redis + BullMQ over a managed queue for CUR processing
context: Cost & Usage Report processing is long-running, lumpy, and needs visible progress. A user uploads a report and waits; a worker dying mid-job must not silently restart the whole thing.
decision: Redis with BullMQ for scheduling and orchestration of report processing.

alternatives.why: Rejected for this path — the 15-minute ceiling and weak progress reporting fit poorly with jobs that run for minutes and need a progress bar. Still used elsewhere in the stack for short work.
Rejected — ties a multi-minute job to an HTTP connection, which fails the first time a load balancer disagrees.

consequence: We own retry semantics and dead-letter handling rather than inheriting them. That is real operational work, bought in exchange for resumability and progress the user can see.

title: One Fargate task per scanner
context: Three third-party security scanners with very different runtimes, dependency trees and failure modes, run against untrusted repositories and websites.
decision: Deploy each scanner as its own isolated Fargate task.

alternatives.why: Rejected — a dependency conflict between two scanners becomes an outage for all three, and one crash loses the whole scan.
Rejected — scanning is bursty and untrusted; per-scan isolation on demand is both cheaper and safer than a warm host accumulating state.

consequence: Higher per-scan startup cost and three sets of task definitions to maintain. Bought fault isolation on a path that runs untrusted input by design.

title: Support both CUR upload and delegated read access
context: Getting at a customer's Cost & Usage Report requires either a file from them or credentials into their account. Which of those procurement will approve varies by organisation and is not predictable in advance.
decision: Build both paths and let the customer pick.

alternatives.why: Rejected — the cleaner engineering answer, and it loses every customer whose security team will not grant cross-account read.
Rejected — works for a pilot, then becomes a manual monthly chore that quietly kills retention.

consequence: Two ingestion paths to keep working and test against. Directly removes the most common reason a deal stalls, which made it worth the duplication.
